# Import, Export & Interoperability {#sec-tech-interop}

This chapter documents the mechanisms that make exchanging database files safe:
the portable identity of an allele, the compatibility gate that guards a merge,
the atomic merge itself, the fresh-built export, and the staging area for peer
profiles that can be compared but not fully absorbed.

## Portable identity: the profile lingua franca {#sec-tech-interop-profile}

`app/logic/profile_io.R` reads and writes cgMLST **profile tables** — one row per
isolate, one column per locus, an allele identifier per cell — the format every
tool agrees on in shape but not in detail. It captures those details in
`PROFILE_PRESETS` and distinguishes two identifier kinds:

- **`hash`** — the `sha256` of the allele sequence. The only *portable* identity,
  and what an interoperable export should use (it is also what chewBBACA's
  `--hash-profiles` emits [@silva2018chewbbaca]).
- **`index`** — the integer `sequences.id`. This is pyMLST's *global* sequence id,
  **not** a per-locus allele number, so it is not comparable with conventional
  cgMLST numbering (SeqSphere, cgMLST.org, chewBBACA) and is meaningful only
  inside one database lineage.

The module also cleans foreign inputs on the way in — stripping whitespace and
prefixes such as chewBBACA's `INF-`, and auto-detecting whether a table has loci
in columns or rows (`parse_profile_file()`, `detect_value_kind()`) — and it
assembles export bundles (profile + metadata + per-locus FASTA) for downstream
tools (`export_typing_results()`).

## The compatibility gate {#sec-tech-interop-compat}

Before any merge is offered, `app/logic/db_compat.R` decides whether two
databases are *mergeable at all*. They are only mergeable when both were built
from the **same scheme**: same organism, same scheme identity, same locus set,
and — the strongest signal — the **same reference alleles**. Every connection here
is opened read-only (`connect_ro`).

```{.r filename="app/logic/db_compat.R"}
#' Evaluates whether an external database matches the schema, species, scheme,
#' loci, and reference alleles of the loaded database.
check_import_compatibility <- function(local_path, ext_path) { ... }
```

The reference-allele check catches the hardest case: two databases that agree on
locus *names* but were built from different reference genomes. Because the
synthetic `ref` isolate (@sec-db-key) holds one allele per locus for the seed
genome, comparing its `(gene, sha256(sequence))` set across the two files detects
a mismatch a name-only comparison would miss.

## Merging a peer database {#sec-tech-interop-import}

`app/logic/db_import.R` performs the merge. Its design rests on one schema
property: `seqid` is meaningful only inside the database that assigned it, but
`(gene, sha256(sequence))` identifies an allele anywhere. The merge therefore maps
every external allele onto a local one *by content*, allocating fresh local ids
only for alleles the local database has never seen.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-tech-import
%%| fig-cap: "The import pipeline. Nothing touches the live database until an atomic swap; the displaced original is kept as a timestamped backup."
flowchart TD
  A["Peer .db"] --> G{"db_compat gate<br/>same scheme?"}
  G -- no --> X["Merge disabled"]
  G -- yes --> C["classify_isolate_collisions()<br/>novel / duplicate / clash"]
  C --> P["import_preview()<br/>counts, no writes"]
  P --> R["Resolve per-isolate:<br/>import · skip · rename"]
  R --> M["merge_databases()<br/>on a COPY, one transaction"]
  M --> S[".swap_in(): atomic rename"]
  S --> B["original kept as .bak-*"]
```

Three properties make it safe:

- **Nothing is written to the live database.** The merge runs against a *copy* in
  the same directory, inside a single transaction, and the copy is swapped in with
  an atomic rename only after it commits cleanly (`.swap_in()`).
- **The original is retained** as a timestamped `.bak-*` file for rollback
  (`list_backups()`, `restore_backup()`).
- **Collisions are resolved explicitly.** `classify_isolate_collisions()` labels
  each incoming isolate novel, duplicate or clash; `import_preview()` reports the
  outcome *without writing*; the user resolves each as import, skip or rename
  (`suggest_rename()` offers a free name). Custom fields are adopted only where
  the user says so and the datatypes are compatible (`importable_custom_fields()`).

`app/view/database_import.R` drives this and signals `main.R` on completion, which
raises the "database changed — reload?" prompt (@sec-arch-signals).

## Exporting a subset {#sec-tech-interop-export}

`app/logic/db_export.R` writes a new `.db` holding a chosen set of isolates and a
chosen set of metadata columns — for a peer lab to import, or for pyMLST's
`wgMLST` to open directly.

::: {.callout-important title="Withheld columns are never written — the file is built fresh"}
The destination is *built fresh*, not copied-and-pruned: unselected isolates and
withheld metadata columns are never written to the output at any point, not even
transiently. That matters because the purpose of choosing columns is that some are
confidential. The table DDL is also replayed verbatim from the source's
`sqlite_master` rather than reconstructed with `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT`, which
would silently drop `mlst`'s primary key, its foreign key and its indexes, leaving
a file pyMLST cannot type against.
:::

`export_preview()` reports the isolate/allele/locus counts before writing;
`export_database()` performs the write; optional result tables (classical MLST,
AMR) are included only when present and selected (`available_result_tables()`).

## Staging: profiles for comparison, not absorption {#sec-tech-interop-staging}

A peer may send a *profile table* — allele identifiers, not sequences. Such
isolates can contribute to a distance matrix (Hamming compares identity, not
sequence) but can never become first-class members of the typing database, which
needs the real DNA behind every call. `app/logic/db_staging.R` keeps them in their
own `imported_*` tables, read only by the distance path:

```{.r filename="app/logic/db_staging.R"}
# `mlst`, `sequences`, `hashes` and `metadata` are never touched: the `seqid`
# space stays intact, `hash_database()` keeps working, the `.db` export stays a
# clean clone, and a `.db` merge is unaffected.
```

The linkability question — can an identifier be anchored to a real allele? — is
handled by `resolve_profile()`: a `hash` is portable and usable as-is; an `index`
can be *verified* against this database's `(gene, seqid)` pairs (because it is this
lineage's global id); anything else is unlinkable and flagged. Staged sets fold
into the distance matrix through `phylo.R`'s `imported_sets` argument
(@sec-tech-engines-mst), mapped into the local integer code space on the fly.

## Provenance of origins {#sec-tech-interop-sources}

`app/logic/db_sources.R` tracks where each isolate came from — locally typed vs
imported from a named peer — through two mechanisms: a denormalized
`metadata.source` string that survives CSV round-trips, and a `phylotrace_sources`
registry that issues **stable** labels keyed on the peer's `phylotrace_meta.uuid`
(falling back to a normalized filename). Repeated imports from the same peer keep
their existing label even across file renames; two different databases that happen
to share a filename get disambiguated labels (`partner-lab`, `partner-lab (2)`).

## Chapter summary

- Allele identity is the `sha256` of the sequence; allele *numbers* are
  database-local and never trusted across files.
- `db_compat` gates a merge on same-scheme, same-reference-alleles, read-only.
- `db_import` merges on a copy in one transaction, swaps atomically, and keeps a
  `.bak-*` rollback; collisions are resolved per isolate.
- `db_export` builds the output fresh so withheld data is never written, and
  replays DDL verbatim so the result stays a valid pyMLST database.
- `db_staging` holds peer *profiles* for distance-only use without touching the
  typing tables; `db_sources` gives every isolate a stable origin label.
